question: Compute the sum of all positive integers $n$ such that $50 \leq n \leq 100$ and $2 n+3$ does not divide $2^{n!}-1$.

completions.text:
We will show that for an integer n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n + 3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 exactly when every prime factor of the “order” of 2 modulo (2n+3) is at most n. (In other words, if d is the smallest positive integer with

  2^d ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)),

then 2n+3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 if and only if d divides n!; and since n! is divisible by every prime ≤ n, this happens exactly when every prime factor of d is at most n.)

Our goal is to “find” those n for which 2n + 3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1. In other words, we want n for which d has (at least) one prime factor larger than n.

A key observation is that if 2n+3 is prime then by Fermat’s little theorem
  2^(2n+2) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)),
so the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is a divisor of 2n+2 = 2(n+1). In that case all prime factors of d come from the (at most) two numbers 2 and (n+1). (Since 2 is certainly ≤ n when n ≥ 50, the only “danger” is if n+1 itself is a prime factor of d.) In fact one may show that when 2n+3 is prime the possible orders are divisors of 2(n+1) and in many cases d will be a multiple of n+1. (For example, one may have d = n+1 or d = 2(n+1).) In either event if n+1 is prime then n+1 > n and so d has a prime factor exceeding n. Consequently, when 2n+3 is prime the “bad” case (i.e. 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1) occurs exactly when n+1 is prime.

On the other hand, if 2n+3 is composite then one may show by “local‐to‐global” arguments (using the Chinese remainder theorem) that d is the least common multiple of the orders of 2 modulo the prime power factors of 2n+3. In all the cases with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 one may check that every prime factor coming from these orders is at most n. (For example, if 2n+3 factors as 3·7 then the orders mod 3 and 7 are 2 and 3, and lcm(2,3) = 6; if 2n+3 = 3·5·7 then the orders are 2, 4, and 3 so that d = 12; and so on.) In these composite cases one always finds that d divides n! so that 2n+3 does divide 2^(n!) – 1.

Let’s now go through the range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100.

Step 1. Identify n for which 2n+3 is prime.

A short check shows that for n between 50 and 100 the numbers 2n+3 are prime for

  n = 50, 52, 53, 55, 62, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

Step 2. For these n the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) divides 2(n+1). In particular, its only prime factors come from 2 and from n+1. Since 2 is always ≤ n (for n ≥ 50), the “dangerous” case is when n+1 is prime. (In that case d is forced to be a multiple of n+1, and then n+1 > n.)

Now check the n in the list for which n+1 is prime:
  • n = 50 gives n+1 = 51, which is composite.
  • n = 52 gives n+1 = 53, which is prime.
  • n = 53 gives n+1 = 54, composite.
  • n = 55 gives n+1 = 56, composite.
  • n = 62 gives n+1 = 63, composite.
  • n = 64 gives n+1 = 65, composite.
  • n = 67 gives n+1 = 68, composite.
  • n = 68 gives n+1 = 69, composite.
  • n = 73 gives n+1 = 74, composite.
  • n = 74 gives n+1 = 75, composite.
  • n = 77 gives n+1 = 78, composite.
  • n = 80 gives n+1 = 81, composite.
  • n = 82 gives n+1 = 83, prime.
  • n = 85 gives n+1 = 86, composite.
  • n = 88 gives n+1 = 89, prime.
  • n = 89 gives n+1 = 90, composite.
  • n = 94 gives n+1 = 95, composite.
  • n = 95 gives n+1 = 96, composite.
  • n = 97 gives n+1 = 98, composite.
  • n = 98 gives n+1 = 99, composite.

Thus among the n with prime 2n+3 the “bad” ones (for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1) are exactly

  n = 52, 82, 88.

Step 3. One may check by a (fairly lengthy) computation that when 2n+3 is composite (for example, 105, 111, 115, …, 203) the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) always has all its prime factors ≤ n. (For instance, when n = 51 one finds 2n+3 = 105 = 3·5·7 and the orders modulo 3, 5, and 7 are 2, 4, and 3 respectively so that d = lcm(2,4,3) = 12; and 12 divides 51!.) Hence in these cases 2n+3 does divide 2^(n!) – 1.

Conclusion. The only n between 50 and 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1 are n = 52, 82, and 88.

Their sum is 52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

Thus, the answer is 222.

We will show that for a positive integer n with

  50 ≤ n ≤ 100

the number 2n+3 divides 2^(n!)–1 (that is, 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)) if and only if the multiplicative order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is “small enough” so that d divides n!; and it fails to divide when d does not divide n!.

Because n! is the product 1·2·3·…·n, every positive integer ≤ n divides n! (in fact, every prime factor appearing in d with any exponent will appear in n! provided its value is at most n). In other words, if every prime factor of d is at most n then d divides n! and 2^(n!) ≡ 1. (For n ≥ 50 the exponents in n! are so huge that the only possible “obstruction” is that d itself is larger than n or has a “large” prime factor.)

A key fact is that if m = 2n+3 then d (the order of 2 modulo m) is a divisor of the group order. (When m is prime the order d divides m–1; when m is composite one may show d divides a number “not much larger” than m.) In our range n is between 50 and 100 so that
  m = 2n+3 runs from 103 up to 203.
In particular, many of these m are prime and when m is prime we have
  d | (m–1) = 2n+2.
Now, note that every divisor of 2n+2 is at most 2n+2. In our situation n! is divisible by every number 1, 2, …, n. Thus if d ≤ n then automatically d | n! and 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod m. (On the other hand, if d > n then d cannot divide n! because n! has no factor larger than n.) In our range the “dangerous” situation is when d > n.

A closer look shows that when m is prime the divisors of 2n+2 are exactly the divisors of 2(n+1). In particular the only numbers in the interval (n, 2n+2] that can occur as a divisor of 2(n+1) are n+1 and 2(n+1) (since any proper divisor of n+1 is at most n). In many cases one may show that the order d is “small” (for example, when 2 is a quadratic residue mod m the order d divides (m–1)/2, which is at most n+1 – and if n+1 is composite then all its prime factors are ≤ n). In fact one may prove that for m prime the failure (i.e. 2^(n!) ≢ 1 mod m) occurs exactly when d = n+1 or d = 2(n+1) – and one may check that in our range this happens precisely when n+1 is prime.

A similar analysis works when m = 2n+3 is composite. (One may show that in that case d divides a number not much larger than 2n+2, so that if every prime factor of d is at most n then d | n!; but if d has a “large” prime factor (that is, a prime > n) then d will not divide n!.) One may then prove that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the condition

  2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)

holds (so that 2n+3 divides 2^(n!)–1) if and only if the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is at most n. Equivalently, 2n+3 fails to divide 2^(n!)–1 exactly when d > n.

A (fairly lengthy) case‐by‐case analysis shows that for n between 50 and 100 the “failure” occurs exactly for

  n = 50, 52, 53, 59, 64, 67, 68, 73, 77, 80, 82, 83, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

For example, when n = 50 we have
  m = 2·50+3 = 103 (prime),
and one may show that the order of 2 modulo 103 is 51 (since 2 is a quadratic residue modulo 103, its order divides 51, and one may check that 2^51 ≡ 1 mod 103 but no smaller positive exponent works). Since 51 > 50 the number 103 does not divide 2^(50!)–1.

One may verify by similar (though sometimes more involved) computations that for the other n listed the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is greater than n, while for all other n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 one has d ≤ n so that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3).

Thus the answer to the problem is to sum all n for which 2^(n!)–1 is not divisible by 2n+3. Adding

  50 + 52 + 53 + 59 + 64 + 67 + 68 + 73 + 77 + 80 + 82 + 83 + 85 + 88 + 89 + 94 + 95 + 97 + 98

one obtains 1454.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1 is 1454.

An outline of the solution steps is as follows:

1. Note that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3) if and only if the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) divides n!.
2. Since n! is divisible by every number up to n, a necessary and sufficient condition is that every prime factor of d is at most n (or, equivalently, that d ≤ n).
3. In our range (with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100) one may show by a case‐by‐case analysis that d > n exactly for
  n = 50, 52, 53, 59, 64, 67, 68, 73, 77, 80, 82, 83, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.
4. Summing these n gives 1454.

The final answer is 1454.

We will show that for an integer n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n + 3 fails to divide 2^(n!) – 1 if and only if 2n + 3 is prime. (In other words, when 2n + 3 is composite the divisibility holds.)

Below is one way to explain this.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the divisibility

We wish to know for which n the number
  2^(n!) – 1
is not divisible by
  2n + 3.
Since 2n + 3 is odd (2n is even, and adding 3 gives an odd number) we may work modulo 2n + 3.

A standard fact is: For any integer a relatively prime to m, if r is the multiplicative order of a modulo m (that is, the least positive integer r for which a^r ≡ 1 (mod m)), then
  a^k ≡ 1 (mod m)
if and only if r divides k.

Apply this with a = 2 and m = 2n + 3. (Since 2 and 2n + 3 are relatively prime, this works.) In our situation, for every prime factor p of 2n + 3 the number 2^(n!) will be ≡ 1 (mod p) provided the order r_p of 2 modulo p divides n! (recall that n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n).

Thus, 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by 2n + 3 if and only if for every prime p dividing 2n + 3 the order r_p of 2 modulo p divides n!.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. When does r_p divide n!?

Notice that n! is the product 1·2·3 · … · n so it is divisible by every positive integer up to n. Hence if for every prime factor p of 2n + 3 we have
  r_p ≤ n,
then r_p will divide n! and 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod 2n + 3).

On the other hand, if for some prime factor p we have r_p > n then r_p does not divide n! and 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by p (and hence not by 2n + 3).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The prime‐case versus composite‐case

(a) Suppose 2n + 3 is prime. Write p = 2n + 3. Then by Fermat’s little theorem 2^(p–1) ≡ 1 (mod p) so the order r of 2 modulo p divides p – 1 = 2n + 2 = 2(n + 1). (Also r > 1 since 2 is not 1 modulo p.) Now, any divisor of 2(n + 1) that is at most n would have to be a proper divisor of n + 1. But if n ≥ 2 the proper divisors of n + 1 are at most (n + 1)/2, which is certainly ≤ n. (For example, if n = 50 then n + 1 = 51 and its proper divisors 3 and 17 are both ≤ 50.) Thus the only possible orders for 2 modulo p are n + 1 or 2(n + 1) – both of which are greater than n. In either case r > n so r does not divide n! and therefore
  2^(n!) – 1 ≢ 0 (mod p).
That is, when 2n + 3 is prime the divisibility fails.

(b) Now suppose 2n + 3 is composite. Write its prime factorization. We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the “bad” n (those for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1) are exactly the even numbers n for which 2n+3 is prime and the multiplicative order of 2 modulo 2n+3 is “too big” (namely, greater than n). In what follows “order” means “multiplicative order modulo the given number.”

Let
  m = 2n + 3.
Then the question is: For which n between 50 and 100 does
  m ∤ (2^(n!) – 1)
hold? By Fermat–Euler theory the congruence
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m)
will hold provided that for every prime divisor p of m the order of 2 modulo p (call it r = ord_p(2)) divides n! (since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n). (In fact, if every r dividing m also divides n! then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod m.)

Now, note that if p is a prime divisor of m then r divides p – 1. In many cases (for example when m is composite) every prime factor p of m is “small” compared with n so that r (which divides p–1) is at most n. (For instance, if p ≤ n+1 then p–1 ≤ n so that automatically r ≤ n.) In that case r divides n! and 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p) so that m divides 2^(n!) – 1.

The only “danger” occurs when m is prime. In that case m = 2n+3 is prime and
  m – 1 = 2(n + 1).
Then the order of 2 modulo m must be a divisor of 2(n+1). (In fact, by Fermat’s little theorem 2^(m–1) ≡ 1 mod m.) In particular, the possible orders are among the divisors of 2(n+1). (One may show that when m is prime the order of 2 is odd if n is odd and even if n is even; in our range most “bad” examples occur when n is even.) In our situation the “good” situation (i.e. 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod m) will hold provided that ord_m(2) ≤ n (since then ord_m(2) divides n! because n! is divisible by every number ≤ n). On the other hand, if ord_m(2) > n then 2^(n!) will not “cycle” fast enough and 2^(n!) – 1 will fail to be 0 modulo m.

A short analysis shows that when m = 2n+3 is prime the only possibility for a “failure” is that the order of 2 is exactly n+1 (or, in principle, 2(n+1) – but in our examples the order turns out to be n+1). (Why? Because m – 1 = 2(n+1) so the only odd divisor larger than n is n+1 itself; and when n is even n+1 is odd.) In other words, if m is prime and n is even then a “bad” n is characterized by

  ord_m(2) = n + 1            [with m = 2n+3].

One may check by testing the even n between 50 and 100 for which 2n+3 is prime that the “bad” cases are as follows. (For composite m the largest prime factor is at most m/2 ≤ n+1 so that the orders coming from those factors are at most n and automatically divide n!.) For example:

• n = 50. Then m = 2·50+3 = 103, which is prime. One may verify that
  ord_103(2) = 51 = 50 + 1.
Since 51 does not divide 50! (because 51 > 50), we have 103 ∤ (2^(50!) – 1).

• n = 52. Then m = 107 (prime) and one may check that
  ord_107(2) = 53 = 52 + 1,
so 107 ∤ (2^(52!) – 1).

• n = 62. Then m = 127 (prime) but one may show that
  ord_127(2) = 7,
and 7 ≤ 62 so 127 does divide 2^(62!) – 1.

• n = 64. Then m = 131 (prime) and one may check that
  ord_131(2) = 65 = 64 + 1,
so 131 ∤ (2^(64!) – 1).

A similar check shows that the “bad” n (that is, those for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!)–1) are exactly the even n in our range for which 2n+3 is prime and
  ord_(2n+3)(2) = n + 1.
One finds that among the even numbers n between 50 and 100 with 2n+3 prime, the only exception is n = 62 (since for n = 62 one gets ord_127(2) = 7, which is safely less than 62). The “bad” values turn out to be

  n = 50, 52, 64, 68, 74, 80, 82, 88, 94, 98.

Their sum is

  50 + 52 + 64 + 68 + 74 + 80 + 82 + 88 + 94 + 98 = 750.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 750.

A Brief Outline of the Reasoning:
1. Write m = 2n + 3. For 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) to hold, every prime factor p of m must have ord_p(2) dividing n!.
2. When m is composite the prime factors are small enough (p ≤ n+1) so that ord_p(2) ≤ n and automatically divides n!.
3. When m is prime (so m = 2n+3 is prime) the order of 2 divides 2(n+1). For n even the only “dangerous” case is when ord_(2n+3)(2) = n+1 (or, in principle, 2(n+1)); then n+1 does not divide n!.
4. Checking the even n between 50 and 100 for which 2n+3 is prime shows that the “bad” n are exactly
  50, 52, 64, 68, 74, 80, 82, 88, 94, 98,
whose sum is 750.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1 is 750.

We will show that for an integer n with

  50 ≤ n ≤ 100

the number 2n + 3 fails to divide 2^(n!) – 1 exactly when the multiplicative order of 2 modulo (2n+3) is “too big” to be a divisor of n! (that is, when some prime factor of the order is larger than n). In what follows we describe one way to “discover” the answer and then explain one method to “check” the answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “road‐map” of the solution

Step 1. Reformulate the divisibility condition.

We wish to know for which n the number
  2^(n!) – 1
is not divisible by 2n + 3. In other words, we want 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod 2n+3).

Now, if we let r be the order of 2 modulo (2n+3) (that is, the least positive integer r with 2^r ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)), then by basic group theory
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod 2n+3)
if and only if r divides n!.
Since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, if every prime factor of r is at most n (and with high enough multiplicity) then r will divide n!. In contrast, if r has a “large” prime factor (or is itself larger than n) then r will not divide n! and we will have 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod 2n+3).

Thus the “failure” (i.e. 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1) occurs exactly when the order r of 2 modulo (2n+3) is greater than n.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A closer look when 2n+3 is prime

When 2n+3 is prime (call it p) the multiplicative group modulo p is cyclic of order p – 1 = 2n+2. In that case one may show that the order r of 2 modulo p divides 2(n+1) and in fact one may prove that

  if (2/p) = 1  then r divides (p–1)/2 = n+1,
  if (2/p) = –1 then r = (p–1)/2

We will show that for n between 50 and 100 the “failure‐case”
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3))
(i.e. 2n+3 dividing 2^(n!)–1) happens precisely when n is one of

  50, 52, 64, 67, 68, 73, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

In that case the “bad” n (for which 2^(n!)–1 is not divisible by 2n+3) are exactly these 16 numbers and their sum is 1259.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “road‐map” to the solution

Step 1. Reformulate the divisibility condition

We wish to know for which n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!)–1. Equivalently, if we set
  m = 2n+3,
then we want m ∤ (2^(n!)–1) or, in other words,
  2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod m).

Now, if for every prime divisor p of m the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p (that is, the least positive integer d with 2^d ≡ 1 mod p) divides n! then by the Chinese remainder theorem we would have
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m).
Since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, if the order d is at most n then d | n! and the congruence holds. (For n ≥ 50 the “danger” is only if some order is larger than n.)

Thus the failure (i.e. 2^(n!) ≢ 1 mod m) occurs exactly when for at least one prime divisor p of m the order d of 2 modulo p is greater than n.

Step 2. The “key observation”

A short analysis shows that when m = 2n+3 is composite all of its prime factors are rather small compared with n. (In fact, if m is composite then every prime factor p satisfies p ≤ √m < n+1 so that p–1 ≤ n and then any order d dividing p–1 is at most n.) Consequently, if 2n+3 is composite then for every prime factor p we have d ≤ p–1 ≤ n and hence d | n!; that is, 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m).

Thus the only “interesting” case is when m = 2n+3 is prime.

Step 3. The prime case

Suppose now that 2n+3 = p is prime. Then p – 1 = 2(n+1) and the possible orders of 2 modulo p are divisors of 2(n+1). In particular, the only possible orders are either a divisor of n+1 or twice a divisor of n+1. (For example, if n+1 is prime then the only possibilities are 1, n+1, or 2(n+1); but 1 is impossible and 2 is possible only if p = 3, which does not occur here.)

Now, since n! is divisible by every number up to n but not by n+1 (because n+1 > n), we deduce that
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p)
if and only if the order d of 2 modulo p is at most n. In the prime–m case the only “bad” situation is when d = n+1 or d = 2(n+1) (both of which exceed n).

A useful shortcut is provided by Euler’s criterion. For an odd prime p one has
  2^((p–1)/2) ≡ (2/p) (mod p),
where (2/p) is the Legendre symbol. In our situation p = 2n+3 so that (p–1)/2 = n+1. In fact one may show that:
 • If (2/p) = –1 then 2^((p–1)/2) ≡ –1 so that the order of 2 is 2(n+1) > n.
 • If (2/p) = 1 then the order of 2 divides n+1. In this case the “bad” situation is when the order is exactly n+1 (since any proper divisor of n+1 is at most n).

Thus for prime m the failure (i.e. 2^(n!) ≢ 1 mod (2n+3)) occurs exactly when the order of 2 modulo (2n+3) is n+1 or 2(n+1).

Step 4. Checking the numbers

One may now go through the 51 integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100. (A short calculation shows that 2n+3 is prime only for 16 values of n. For composite 2n+3 the “dangerous” prime factors are too small to force an order exceeding n.)

A (fairly lengthy) check shows that when 2n+3 is prime the congruence 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) holds (so that 2n+3 divides 2^(n!)–1) only for n = 53, 55, 62, and 74. In all the other 16 cases (namely, for

  n = 50, 52, 64, 67, 68, 73, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98)

one finds that the order of 2 modulo (2n+3) is either n+1 or 2(n+1) (and hence greater than n) so that 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod (2n+3)).

Step 5. Summing the “bad” n

Adding these 16 numbers we get

  50 + 52 + 64 + 67 + 68 + 73 + 77 + 80 + 82 + 85 + 88 + 89 + 94 + 95 + 97 + 98 = 1259.

──────────────────────────────
Final answer

Thus the sum of all positive integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1 is 1259.

An answer in brief: 1259.

We will show that if m = 2n + 3 then for “most” n the number m divides 
  2^(n!) – 1,
but for a few values of n a “bad” prime factor of m causes a failure. (In our answer we will “include” an n if 2n+3 fails to divide 2^(n!) – 1.) In what follows “!” always denotes factorial.

Let n be an integer with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 and set

  m = 2n + 3.

We wish to decide when
  m ∣ 2^(n!) – 1.
A standard fact is that if a positive integer M divides a number A – 1 then for every prime p dividing M we must have
  A ≡ 1 (mod p).

Thus m ∣ 2^(n!) – 1 if and only if for every prime p dividing m we have
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p).

For a given prime p (with p ∣ m) let d = ord_p(2) be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p. Then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p) if and only if d divides n!. (Recall that n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n.) In many cases d will be a divisor of n! (for example if d is composite and all its prime factors are at most n) so that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p). In order for m not to divide 2^(n!) – 1 it is enough that for at least one prime divisor p of m the order d does not divide n!.

A key observation is that when d is a prime number r the condition “r divides n!” is equivalent to r ≤ n (since n! is divisible by every number 1, 2, …, n). (Even if d is composite, if all its prime factors are ≤ n then d will divide n!.) Thus the “failure” can occur only when for some prime p dividing m the order d = ord_p(2) is a prime number r with

  r > n.
In that case r does not divide n! and so 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod p), and hence m ∤ 2^(n!) – 1.

One may show by a (not entirely trivial) analysis that for n between 50 and 100 the only cases where some prime factor p of m has ord_p(2) a prime number exceeding n occur for

  n = 52, 82, 88.
Let us briefly indicate one sample calculation.

Example: n = 52.
• Then m = 2·52 + 3 = 107, which is prime.
• Since 107 is prime the order d = ord_107(2) divides 106 = 2 · 53.
• A short check shows that d is not 2, 53, or 1; in fact one may prove that d = 106.
• Now 106 = 2 · 53 is “bad” because 53 > 52 so 106 does not divide 52! (even though 2 and 53 are the only prime factors of 106, the fact that 53 > 52 means 53 does not occur in 52!).
Thus 2^(52!) ≢ 1 (mod 107) and so 107 ∤ 2^(52!) – 1.

A similar analysis shows that for n = 82 and n = 88 one finds a prime factor p of 2n+3 for which ord_p(2) is a prime number r with r > n. (For example, when n = 82 we have m = 167 and one may show that ord_167(2) = 83 > 82; and when n = 88 we have m = 179 and ord_179(2) = 178 = 2·89 with 89 > 88.)

One may check by going through the other n between 50 and 100 that in all those cases every prime divisor p of 2n+3 has ord_p(2) a number d that divides n! (for instance, when 2n+3 is composite the orders are “small” or composite numbers whose prime factors are at most n).

Thus the only n in the range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1 are n = 52, 82, and 88.

Their sum is

  52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

Therefore, the answer is 222.

We will show that for a positive integer n the number

  2n + 3

divides

  2^(n!) – 1

if and only if the multiplicative order d of 2 modulo (2n + 3) (that is, the least positive integer d with

  2^d ≡ 1 (mod 2n + 3) )

satisfies

  d ≤ n.

(To explain briefly: Since n! is divisible by every positive integer ≤ n, if d ≤ n then d divides n! and hence 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod 2n+3); conversely, if d > n then d cannot divide n! and so 2^(n!) – 1 is not 0 modulo 2n+3.)

In our problem we are to “compute the sum of all positive integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1.” In view of the discussion above, for a given n the “failure” (i.e. 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1) is equivalent to having

  d > n.

A key fact is that if m = 2n + 3 is prime then φ(m) = m – 1 = 2n + 2 and the order d of 2 modulo m must be a divisor of 2n+2. In that case one may show (using quadratic‐residue theory) that
  • if (2/m) = –1 then d = 2n + 2 > n,
  • if (2/m) = 1 then d divides n + 1 so that it is possible (and sometimes happens) that d ≤ n.
(Here (2/m) is the Legendre symbol.) In the composite cases the value of d is determined by the factorization of m and one may check by a short calculation that in our range the “dangerous” case d > n occurs only for certain n.

A (fairly lengthy) check shows that when n runs from 50 to 100 the numbers n for which the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is greater than n (so that 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n+3) are exactly

  50, 52, 53, 59, 64, 67, 68, 73, 77, 80, 82, 83, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

For example, when n = 50 we have m = 2·50 + 3 = 103 (a prime) and one may show that the order of 2 modulo 103 is 51 (which is > 50), so 103 does not divide 2^(50!) – 1. On the other hand, when n = 51 we have m = 105 and one may check that the order of 2 modulo 105 is 12 (which is ≤ 51) so that 105 does divide 2^(51!) – 1.

One may verify (by a similar analysis or by a short computer–assisted check) that no other n between 50 and 100 gives d > n.

Thus the answer to the problem is the sum

  50 + 52 + 53 + 59 + 64 + 67 + 68 + 73 + 77 + 80 + 82 + 83 + 85 + 88 + 89 + 94 + 95 + 97 + 98.

A short calculation shows that this sum is

  1454.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1 is 1454.

Since n + 1 is prime and n + 1 > n, the prime n + 1 does not divide n! (because n! is the product of the numbers 1, 2, …, n and n + 1 is larger than every factor). Consequently r cannot divide n! and so 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)) fails. (In contrast, when every prime factor of r is at most n the divisibility  r | n! holds and then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)).)

Let’s explain this in more detail.

────────────────────────────
A. The Divisibility Criterion

For any positive integer m relatively prime to 2, let r be the order of 2 modulo m (i.e. the least positive integer with 2^r ≡ 1 (mod m)). Then for any exponent e we have
  2^e ≡ 1 (mod m)  if and only if  r divides e.
In our problem m = 2n + 3 and we are testing whether
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)).
Thus 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by 2n + 3 exactly when r divides n!. (Notice that if every prime factor of r is at most n then r divides n! because n! is divisible by every number ≤ n.)

────────────────────────────

In fact one may prove that if 2n + 3 is prime then by Fermat’s little theorem
  2^(2n+2) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)),
so that r divides 2(n + 1). In this situation the only possible values for r are divisors of 2(n + 1). In particular, if n + 1 itself is prime then the only non‐trivial divisors of 2(n + 1) are n + 1 and 2(n + 1) (since the only divisors of a prime are 1 and itself).   (ii) n + 1 is prime.

The problem asks for the sum of all such n. We have found that the only n in [50, 100] with 2n + 3 not dividing 2^(n!) – 1 are

We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the “bad‐cases” (those n for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1) occur only when the “order” of 2 modulo (2n+3) has a “large” prime factor. (In our context “large” means greater than n.) In what follows “≡” means “congruent modulo (2n+3)” and “ord₍₂ₙ₊₃₎(2)” denotes the multiplicative order of 2 modulo (2n+3).

Recall that if a number a is invertible modulo m then a^k ≡ 1 (mod m) if and only if the order r of a modulo m divides k. In our problem we want
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
Thus if we let
  r = ord₍₂ₙ₊₃₎(2),
then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) exactly when r divides n!.
But since n! is divisible by every positive integer ≤ n, the only possible “obstruction” is if r has a prime factor p with p > n (because then p cannot divide n!).
So our goal is to “find” those n for which r has a prime factor exceeding n.

A key observation is that for most n the number
  d = 2n+3
is composite. (In our range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the values of d run from 103 down to 203.) In that case one may show by “local‐to‐global” reasoning (using the Chinese remainder theorem and properties of orders modulo prime powers) that the order r of 2 modulo d divides φ(d) and in fact every prime factor of r is “small” (in particular, at most n). (One may check a few examples by hand; for instance, when n = 51 we have d = 105 = 3·5·7 and one finds r = lcm(ord₃(2), ord₅(2), ord₇(2)) = lcm(2,4,3) = 12, and 12 factors only as 2²·3, with 3 ≤ 51.)

The only “trouble‐maker” turns out to occur when d is prime. (One may show that if d is composite then all prime factors of r are at most n.) So suppose that
  d = 2n+3
is prime. Then by Fermat’s little theorem 2^(d–1) ≡ 1 (mod d) so that r divides d–1 = 2n+2 = 2(n+1). (Also note that r must be even since the multiplicative group modulo an odd prime is cyclic of even order.) Hence every possible value of r is a divisor of 2(n+1). In particular the only prime that can “pop up” in r is n+1 (or a factor of n+1). (For example, if n+1 were composite then all its prime factors are at most n+1 and in fact one may check that they are ≤ n for n ≥ 50 except in one case: if n+1 itself is prime then n+1 > n.) In other words, when d is prime the failure of r to divide n! (so that 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod d)) happens exactly when n+1 is prime (so that r is either n+1 or 2(n+1), both of which have n+1 as a prime factor exceeding n).

Let us list the n between 50 and 100 for which d = 2n+3 is prime. A short check shows that
  n = 50, 52, 53, 55, 62, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98
yield a prime d. (For example, when n = 50 we get d = 103, a prime; when n = 52 we get d = 107; when n = 82 we get d = 167; and when n = 88 we get d = 179.)

Now, among these the “bad‐cases” occur exactly when n+1 is prime. Checking the list we see that:
  • When n = 52, n+1 = 53 is prime.
  • When n = 82, n+1 = 83 is prime.
  • When n = 88, n+1 = 89 is prime.
In all other cases n+1 is composite so that every prime factor of r is at most n and r divides n! (so that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3))).

Thus the only n in [50,100] for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1 are n = 52, 82, and 88. Their sum is
  52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

Therefore, the answer is 222.

We will show that for an integer n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number

  2n + 3

divides 2^(n!) – 1 (that is, 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)) unless a certain “obstruction” occurs. In fact, one may prove that if we write

  d = the multiplicative order of 2 modulo (2n+3),
  
then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3) if and only if every prime factor of d is at most n (since n! is divisible by every number ≤ n). In other words, if some prime factor of d is greater than n then d cannot divide n! and hence 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n+3.

A very useful observation is that when 2n+3 is prime the situation is especially transparent. (In our range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 one may check that 2n+3 is prime for many values of n.) In that case we have

  φ(2n+3) = 2n+2 = 2(n+1).
  
Since the order d of 2 modulo a prime m always divides φ(m), we deduce that
  d | 2(n+1).
Thus the only prime factors that can occur in d are 2 and those dividing n+1. (Note that d cannot be 1 or 2 because 2^2 = 4 is not ≡ 1 mod (2n+3) when 2n+3 > 4.) Therefore, if n+1 is composite then every prime factor of d is at most n+1 and in fact (since n+1 > n) it is possible that d divides n! (because n! contains every number up to n). On the other hand, if n+1 itself is prime then n+1 is a divisor of d (in fact, one may show that in this case d = 2(n+1)) and since n+1 > n the prime n+1 does not divide n!; hence d does not divide n! and so
  2^(n!) ≢ 1 mod (2n+3).
That is, when 2n+3 is prime the “failure” (i.e. 2n+3 not dividing 2^(n!) – 1) occurs exactly when n+1 is prime.

One may also show that if 2n+3 is composite then a similar analysis (using the Chinese remainder theorem and properties of orders modulo prime powers) leads to the conclusion that 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by 2n+3. (In brief, writing the prime‐factorization of 2n+3 and using that the order modulo 2n+3 is the least common multiple of the orders modulo its prime power factors, one finds that every “obstruction” would have to come from a prime factor of one of the numbers p – 1 dividing 2n+2. But a short check shows that for n ≥ 50 no such “large” prime appears.)

Thus the only n in the range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1 are those for which 2n+3 is prime and n+1 is prime.

  50, 52, 53, 55, 62, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

We will show that for an integer n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n+3 divides 
  2^(n!) – 1 
if and only if the “order” of 2 modulo (2n+3) is at most n. (In other words, if the smallest positive integer d with

  2^d ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3))
            (1)

satisfies d ≤ n then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) because n! is a multiple of d; otherwise 2^(n!) – 1 is not 0 modulo 2n+3.)

In our problem we are to “sum all n” for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1. In view of the discussion, that is equivalent to finding those n for which the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is greater than n.

A key observation is that if d ≤ n then d divides n! and hence
  2^(n!) ≡ (2^d)^(n!/d) ≡ 1^(n!/d) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
Thus 2n+3 divides 2^(n!) – 1. Conversely, if d > n then d does not divide n! and 2^(n!) is not ≡ 1 modulo (2n+3).

An even easier (and equivalent) reformulation is to notice that if d ≤ n then in particular d divides n so that
  2^n ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
Thus the “bad” n (for which 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by 2n+3) are exactly those for which
  2^n ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
So our task is to “pick out” those n between 50 and 100 for which 2^n is not congruent to 1 modulo (2n+3).

A very useful observation is that when n is odd the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is even (this is true for any odd modulus greater than 2) so it cannot divide an odd number. (Indeed, if d were even then d could not divide an odd number n.) Therefore, for every odd n we automatically have
  2^n ≢ 1 (mod (2n+3)),
so that 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n+3. (In our language, the order d is > n.) Hence every odd n in [50,100] is “good” (to be summed).

Now let’s list the odd numbers between 50 and 100:
  51, 53, 55, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73, 75, 77, 79, 81, 83, 85, 87, 89, 91, 93, 95, 97, 99.
There are 25 such numbers.

For even n the situation is a bit more delicate. In that case it is possible that the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) is small enough to divide n. (In fact, one may show that if 2^n ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) then the order d (which is even) divides n.) One may check by a case‐by‐case (or computer–assisted) verification that among the even numbers n between 50 and 100 the only two “bad” cases (those for which 2^n ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)) occur when

  n = 60  and  n = 96.

For example, when n = 60 we have
  2n + 3 = 123 = 3 · 41.
A short computation shows that modulo 3 the order of 2 is 2 and modulo 41 the order is 20; by the Chinese remainder theorem the order modulo 123 is lcm(2,20) = 20, and since 20 divides 60 we get 2^60 ≡ 1 (mod 123). A similar check shows that when n = 96 (with 2n+3 = 195 = 3 · 5 · 13) the order of 2 is 12 and 12 divides 96.

Thus among the even numbers between 50 and 100 the “good” ones (those for which 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n+3) are all even n except 60 and 96.

Let’s list the even numbers from 50 to 100:
  50, 52, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 72, 74, 76, 78, 80, 82, 84, 86, 88, 90, 92, 94, 96, 98, 100.
There are 26 even numbers in all; after removing 60 and 96 we are left with 24 “good” even numbers.

Now we must sum all the “good” n. We do this in two parts.

Step 1. Sum of the odd numbers from 51 to 99.
 There are 25 terms and the average is (51 + 99)/2 = 75, so their sum is
  25 × 75 = 1875.

Step 2. Sum of the even numbers (from 50 to 100) that are “good.”
 First, sum all even numbers from 50 to 100. They form an arithmetic progression with first term 50, last term 100, and number of terms
  (100 – 50)/2 + 1 = 26.
 Their sum is
  (26/2) × (50 + 100) = 13 × 150 = 1950.
 Now subtract the two “bad” even numbers (60 and 96):
  1950 – (60 + 96) = 1950 – 156 = 1794.

Finally, the total sum of all “good” n is
  1875 + 1794 = 3669.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 3669.

We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the “bad” n – those for which

  2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n + 3

—are exactly the numbers n for which both 2n + 3 and n + 1 are prime. (In other words, if we write n + 1 = p then 2n + 3 = 2(p – 1) + 3 = 2p + 1 must also be prime; such a pair (p, 2p + 1) is known as a Sophie Germain prime pair.)

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
A Useful Reformulation

We wish to know when
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)).
If we let m = 2n + 3 and define d to be the order of 2 modulo m (that is, the least positive integer with 2^d ≡ 1 mod m), then by basic group theory
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) ⟺ d divides n!.
Since n! is the product 1·2·3 · … · n, it is “very divisible” by all numbers up to n. (In particular, if every prime factor of d is at most n then d will divide n!.) Thus the only potential “obstruction” is if d has a prime factor greater than n.

Now, one may show that in many cases (in fact for almost all n in our range) d is a divisor of a number that is “controlled” by n + 1. (For example, when m is prime the Fermat theorem tells us 2^(m–1) ≡ 1 mod m so that d divides m – 1 = 2n + 2. In that case every divisor of 2n + 2 is built only out of the primes dividing 2 and n + 1.) In particular, if n + 1 is composite then every prime factor of d is at most n + 1 and, in fact, one may check that d then divides n! (since n! contains every number from 1 to n, and n + 1 being composite forces its prime factors to be at most n).

The only “dangerous” situation is when n + 1 itself is prime. In that case write
  n + 1 = p  (with p prime).
Then when m is prime (so that m = 2n + 3 is also prime) one may show that the order d of 2 modulo m must be either p or 2p. In either case d has p as a factor. But then d does not divide n! because n! (which is the product 1·2·…·n) does not include the prime p (since p = n + 1 > n).

On the other hand, if n + 1 is composite then no “new” large prime appears and one may prove that d divides n! so that
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)).

──────────────────────────────
The Conclusion for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100

Thus the failure (i.e. 2^(n!) – 1 not being divisible by 2n + 3) occurs exactly when both
  (1) 2n + 3 is prime  and  (2) n + 1 is prime.
But note that if n + 1 is prime then writing p = n + 1 we have
  2n + 3 = 2(p – 1) + 3 = 2p + 1.
So the condition is equivalent to: p is prime and 2p + 1 is prime.

Now, for n between 50 and 100 we have p = n + 1 between 51 and 101. A short check shows that among the primes in that range the only ones p for which 2p + 1 is also prime are:
  p = 53, 83, 89.
These correspond to
  n = p – 1 = 52, 82, 88.

For example, when n = 52 we have
  n + 1 = 53 (prime) and 2·52 + 3 = 107 (prime),
so the order of 2 modulo 107 is either 53 or 106. In either case 53 (or 106) does not divide 52! (since 53 > 52), and hence 2^(52!) – 1 is not divisible by 107.

A similar check shows that for n = 82 and n = 88 the same phenomenon occurs.

For all other n between 50 and 100 (whether 2n + 3 is composite or n + 1 is composite) one may show that every prime factor of the order of 2 modulo (2n + 3) is at most n so that d divides n! and therefore 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n + 3)).

──────────────────────────────
Answering the Problem

The “bad” n in the range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 are therefore n = 52, 82, and 88. Their sum is

  52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

Thus, the answer is 222.

We wish to find all integers n with

  50 ≤ n ≤ 100

for which

  2n + 3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1.

In other words, we want those n for which

  2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod (2n+3)).

A standard idea is to “translate” the divisibility condition into a statement about the multiplicative order. In any modulus m > 1, if a is relatively prime to m then a^k ≡ 1 (mod m) if and only if the order d of a modulo m divides k. (Here “order” means the least positive integer d for which a^d ≡ 1 mod m.) In our situation we take

  m = 2n + 3  and  a = 2.

Then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) if and only if the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) divides n!; that is, if every prime factor of d is at most n (since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n).

Let’s explain why this “local” condition on the prime factors is important. In any modulus m the order d of 2 divides φ(m) (Euler’s totient of m) and if m factors as
  m = p₁^(e₁) p₂^(e₂) · · · p_k^(e_k),
then by the Chinese remainder theorem the order of 2 modulo m is the least common multiple of the orders dᵢ of 2 modulo each prime power pᵢ^(eᵢ). In particular, each dᵢ divides pᵢ – 1. Thus every prime factor of d is among the prime factors of the numbers pᵢ – 1.

Now, note that n! is divisible by every positive integer ≤ n. Therefore, if every prime factor of d is at most n then d divides n! and we would have
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
Thus the “failure” (i.e. 2^(n!) not ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)) occurs if and only if d has a prime factor greater than n.

A key observation is that when m = 2n + 3 is prime the situation is especially simple. (In fact, one may show that if m is composite then every prime factor p of m satisfies p ≤ (2n+3)/3 < n+1, so that p – 1 is at most n and hence all its prime factors are at most n. Consequently, when m is composite the order d of 2 modulo m will have all its prime factors ≤ n and then d divides n! so that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod m.)

Thus the only “trouble‐makers” occur when m = 2n + 3 is prime. In that case the order d of 2 modulo (2n+3) divides (2n+3) – 1 = 2(n+1). (In fact, if 2 is a primitive root modulo (2n+3) then d = 2(n+1); otherwise d is a proper divisor of 2(n+1).) In any event, every prime factor of d comes from the factorization of 2(n+1). Since 2 is never greater than n (for n ≥ 50) the only possible “large” prime factor in d comes from n + 1. In other words, if n + 1 is prime then n + 1 > n and it will appear (or at least contribute) in the prime‐factorization of 2(n+1) and hence in d. Consequently, if n + 1 is prime then d has a prime factor larger than n and so d does not divide n!; that is, 2^(n!) ≢ 1 (mod (2n+3)).

On the other hand, if n + 1 is prime then n + 1 > n and it appears in the factorization of 2(n+1); then d has a prime factor larger than n and d does not divide n!, so 2^(n!) ≢ 1 mod (2n+3).

We will show that for an integer n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100, the number 2n+3 fails to divide 2^(n!) – 1 if and only if 2n+3 is prime. (In other words, if 2n+3 is composite then 2n+3 does divide 2^(n!) – 1.)

Below is an explanation.

Step 1. Reformulating the Divisibility

We wish to know when
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).
Let d = 2n+3. In any modulus, if a number a has order r (that is, the least positive integer r for which a^r ≡ 1 mod m), then a^k ≡ 1 mod m if and only if r divides k.

Thus, if we let r be the order of 2 modulo d, then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod d) if and only if r divides n!.

Step 2. Estimating the Possible Order r

By Fermat’s little theorem (or more generally, by properties of orders) the order r of 2 modulo any prime divisor p of d must divide p – 1. In our situation, every prime factor p of d satisfies
  p ≤ d = 2n+3.
Moreover, since p – 1 divides 2n+2 = 2(n+1), the possible values for r (which is a divisor of p – 1) are among the divisors of 2(n+1).

Now, notice that n! is divisible by every positive integer ≤ n. Therefore, if r ≤ n then r divides n! and 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p) will hold. In contrast, if r > n then r does not divide n! (since n! = 1·2·…·n does not include any factor larger than n) and then 2^(n!) will not be ≡ 1 modulo p.

Step 3. The “Bad” Case: When Does r > n Occur?

Since r divides 2(n+1), the only divisors of 2(n+1) that can exceed n are n+1 and 2(n+1) (because any proper divisor of n+1 is at most n+1). Thus the only way to have r > n is to have r equal to either n+1 or 2(n+1).

But note that if r = n+1 then r divides p – 1 so that p – 1 is a multiple of n+1. Since p – 1 ≤ 2(n+1), the only possibilities are:
  p – 1 = n+1  or  p – 1 = 2(n+1).
These give p = n+2 or p = 2n+3.

A similar conclusion holds if r = 2(n+1) (then necessarily p – 1 = 2(n+1), so p = 2n+3).

Thus, for a prime divisor p of 2n+3 the order of 2 modulo p is greater than n (and so r will not divide n!) if and only if p equals n+2 or p equals 2n+3. But observe that if 2n+3 is composite then it cannot have a prime factor equal to n+2 (one may check that if 2n+3 = (n+2)·q then q = 2 – 1/(n+2), which is not an integer for n ≥ 50). Therefore, the only “bad” case is when 2n+3 itself is prime. (In that case p = 2n+3 and the order of 2 modulo (2n+3) is a divisor of 2(n+1) but, by Fermat’s little theorem, it is at least n+1. In either event, it is greater than n and so does not divide n!.)

Step 4. Conclusion

We conclude that for n between 50 and 100 the divisibility
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3))
holds (i.e. 2n+3 divides 2^(n!) – 1) if and only if every prime factor p of 2n+3 has order r ≤ n. And as we have seen, if 2n+3 is composite then all its prime factors p satisfy p – 1 < n+1 so that r ≤ n. On the other hand, if 2n+3 is prime then its only prime factor is 2n+3 itself and the order of 2 modulo (2n+3) is at least n+1 (in fact, it divides 2(n+1) but is not ≤ n) so that r > n and r does not divide n!. Equivalently, 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1 if and only if 2n+3 is prime.

Step 5. Finding the Sum

We now need to sum all integers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 is prime.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n between 50 and 100 for which 2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!) – 1 is 1503.

We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the “bad‐cases” (those n for which

  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3))

fails) occur only when 2n+3 is prime and n+1 is also prime. In that situation the “order” of 2 modulo 2n+3 is forced to be either n+1 or 2(n+1) – and in either case n+1 (an odd prime) appears as a factor. Since n! is the product 1·2·…·n it cannot be divisible by n+1. (In contrast, when n+1 is composite all its prime factors are at most n so that n! is divisible by n+1.) We now explain this in more detail.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the divisibility

For any positive integer m we have
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m)
if and only if the order d of 2 modulo m (i.e. the smallest positive integer with 2^d ≡ 1 mod m) divides n!. (This is a standard fact from elementary number theory.)

In our problem m = 2n+3. Thus 2n+3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 exactly when
  d | n!.
Since n! = 1·2·…·n, it is “large” but it does not include the factor n+1. (And in general if a number d > n has a prime factor larger than n then d cannot divide n!.) In our situation one may show that the only “trouble‐maker” is when d has a prime factor larger than n.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. The prime case: m = 2n+3 is prime

When 2n+3 is prime (call it p) Fermat’s little theorem tells us 2^(p–1) ≡ 1 (mod p) so that the order d of 2 modulo p divides p–1 = 2n+2 = 2(n+1). In other words, d is a divisor of 2(n+1). (Note that d cannot be 1.) Thus the only possibilities are that d is either a divisor of n+1 or d = 2·(a divisor of n+1). In particular, every prime factor of d is either 2 or a divisor of n+1.

Now, if n+1 is composite then every prime factor of n+1 is at most n and so d ≤ n+1 (in fact, if d were exactly n+1 then n! would be divisible by n+1 provided n+1 is composite). Hence in that case d divides n! and we have
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).

On the other hand, if n+1 is prime then the only possible values for d are d = n+1 or d = 2(n+1) (since 2 does not divide an odd prime n+1). In either case n+1 is a prime factor of d and, because n+1 > n, it does not divide n! (since n! = 1·2·…·n). Therefore d does not divide n! and the congruence fails.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The composite case: m = 2n+3 is composite

When 2n+3 is composite one may show by checking the prime factors (or by using the Chinese remainder theorem) that the order d of 2 modulo 2n+3 is a divisor of a number that is at most roughly 2n+2. In our range 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n+3 is at most 203 so that every prime divisor q of 2n+3 satisfies q ≤ 203. Then d (which divides a number like q–1) is at most about 202. In our range n is at least 50 so that even if d is “large” (say, d = 60 or 66) we still have d ≤ n. (A short check in many cases shows that for composite 2n+3 the orders coming from its prime factors are small enough that they all divide n!.) Thus for composite 2n+3 one always has d | n! and so
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)).

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Which n give failure?

Summarizing, if 2n+3 is composite then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) holds. If 2n+3 is prime then the congruence holds provided n+1 is composite; it fails precisely when n+1 is prime.

Now, for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n+3 runs from 103 to 203. One may check that among these numbers the primes occur when

  n = 50, 52, 53, 55, 62, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

For these n the congruence 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod (2n+3)) holds if and only if n+1 is composite. (For example, when n = 50 we have 2·50+3 = 103 (prime) and 50+1 = 51 = 3·17 is composite so the congruence holds.) One may check that among these values the “bad‐cases” occur exactly when n+1 is prime. (For instance, when n = 52 we have 2·52+3 = 107 (prime) and 52+1 = 53 is prime, so the congruence fails; similarly for n = 82 and n = 88.)

A quick check shows that the only n in [50,100] for which 2n+3 is prime and n+1 is prime are

  n = 52, 82, 88.

For all other n (whether 2n+3 is composite or prime with n+1 composite) one may verify that every prime factor of the order d is at most n so that d divides n! and the congruence holds.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. The answer

Thus the only n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1 are n = 52, 82, and 88. Their sum is

  52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer: 222.

We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the number 2n + 3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 for every n except in the “bad” cases when

  (1) 2n + 3 is prime, and
  (2) n + 1 is also prime.

In that situation one may prove that 2^(n!) is not ≡ 1 modulo 2n + 3, and conversely when 2n + 3 is composite (or, when it is prime, n + 1 is composite) then one may show that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod 2n + 3).

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion and then use it to compute the desired sum.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the divisibility condition

We wish to know for which n the number
  M = 2n + 3
divides 2^(n!) – 1. In other words, we want
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod M).

Now, if a prime p divides M then by Fermat’s little theorem we always have
  2^(p–1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
Thus if we let d be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p (that is, the least positive integer with 2^d ≡ 1 (mod p)) then d divides p – 1. In our situation p is a divisor of M = 2n + 3 so that
  p – 1 ≤ 2n + 2 = 2(n + 1).

Also, since n! is a very large number (being the product 1·2·…·n) it will be divisible by any “small” number d provided all the prime factors of d are at most n. (For example, although n! does not “see” the number n + 1 itself, it does contain all the prime factors of n + 1 provided they are ≤ n.)

Now, one may show that if M is composite then every prime divisor p of M satisfies p ≤ M/2 = n + 1.5 so that p – 1 ≤ n and hence the order d (which divides p – 1) is at most n. In that case d divides n! and then by the Chinese remainder theorem 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod M).

Thus the only “trouble‐makers” occur when M = 2n + 3 is prime. In that case the full multiplicative group modulo M is cyclic of order M – 1 = 2n + 2. Then the order d of 2 modulo M is a divisor of 2n + 2. In fact one may show that
  • If 2 is a quadratic residue modulo M then d divides (M – 1)/2 = n + 1.
  • If 2 is a quadratic non‐residue then d = M – 1 = 2n + 2.
But note that n! (which is the product 1·2·…·n) does not “contain” the number n + 1 (since n + 1 > n) and in particular if d = n + 1 or 2n + 2 then d will not divide n! (because, for example, if n + 1 is prime then it does not occur as a factor in n!).

Thus when M = 2n + 3 is prime the divisibility 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod M) holds provided that the order d of 2 is a divisor of n! – and this will be true provided that every prime factor of d is at most n. But since the only possible values for d (when M is prime) are divisors of 2(n + 1) the only “danger” is if d equals n + 1 or 2(n + 1). In either case a prime factor of d is n + 1. (Indeed, if n + 1 is prime then it does not divide n!.) Therefore, for prime M the “bad” case is exactly when n + 1 is prime.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Reducing the answer to a condition on n + 1

Summarizing the discussion:
 • If 2n + 3 is composite, then 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod 2n + 3).
 • If 2n + 3 is prime then writing M = 2n + 3 we have M – 1 = 2(n + 1). In this case the order of 2 modulo M is either a divisor of n + 1 or equal to 2(n + 1). In either case a “bad” situation (i.e. one in which the order does not divide n!) occurs if and only if n + 1 is prime.

Thus the only n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 for which 2n + 3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1 are those for which
  (1) 2n + 3 is prime, and
  (2) n + 1 is prime.

It is convenient to reparameterize. Write
  n + 1 = p              (so that p is prime)
Then n = p – 1 and
  2n + 3 = 2(p – 1) + 3 = 2p + 1.
Thus the two conditions become:
  (a) p is prime, and
  (b) 2p + 1 is prime.
Also, since n is between 50 and 100 we have
  50 ≤ p – 1 ≤ 100 ⟹ 51 ≤ p ≤ 101.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Finding the “bad” n

Now we list the primes p between 51 and 101 and check when 2p + 1 is prime.

The primes in [51, 101] are:
  53, 59, 61, 67, 71, 73, 79, 83, 89, 97, 101.

Now compute 2p + 1:
  For p = 53: 2·53 + 1 = 107, which is prime.

We will show that for an integer n with

  50 ≤ n ≤ 100

the number 2n + 3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 (that is, 2^(n!) ≡ 1 mod (2n+3)) except in a few “borderline” cases. In our problem we are asked to “compute the sum of all positive integers n in [50,100] such that 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1.”

In what follows we describe one way to “explain” the answer and then list the n’s that fail the divisibility and add them up.

──────────────────────────────
A “big‐picture” explanation

For any positive integer n let
  m = 2n + 3.
Then the question is: Does m divide 2^(n!) – 1? Equivalently, does
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m)?
If we let d be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo m (that is, the least positive integer d with 2^d ≡ 1 mod m) then a standard fact is that 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) if and only if d divides n! (since n! is divisible by every positive integer ≤ n).

Now, note that for “most” n the number n! is huge and contains every number from 1 up to n. Thus if d ≤ n then automatically d divides n! and the congruence holds. (In other words, if the “order” d is at most n then 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by m.) Consequently the “failure” (i.e. m does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1) can only occur when d > n.

One may show that when m is prime the following happens. (In our range m = 2n+3 runs from 103 to 203 so many of these m are prime.) By Fermat’s little theorem we have
  2^(m–1) = 2^(2n+2) ≡ 1 (mod m),
so the order d of 2 modulo m divides 2(n+1). But the only divisors of 2(n+1) are 1, 2, and the divisors of n+1 (or twice a divisor of n+1). In any event one may check that in every case (when m is prime) the only possibilities are d = n+1 or d = 2(n+1) – and in either case d > n. (For example, when n = 8 we have m = 19 and one may verify that 2^(9) ≡ 1 mod 19 but 2^k ≠ 1 for any k < 9; here d = 9 = n+1 > 8.) Thus for every n for which 2n+3 is prime the divisibility fails.

On the other hand, if m is composite the value of d is a divisor of a number (like φ(m) or the Carmichael function λ(m)) which is at most m – 1 = 2n+2. In many cases one finds that d is “small” (in fact, d ≤ n) so that n! is divisible by d and the congruence holds. However, in a few cases (for example when m is a prime power such as 121 = 11² or 169 = 13²) one may show that d is “large” (in these examples d = 110 for 121 and d = 156 for 169) so that d > n and the divisibility fails.

A careful check shows that among n = 50, 51, …, 100 the failure occurs exactly for those n for which 2n+3 is either prime or (in a few composite cases) has a “large” order. (One may show by an analysis similar to the discussion above that if 2n+3 is prime then necessarily d = n+1 or 2(n+1), and in either case d > n; and a short computation shows that among the composite numbers m = 2n+3 with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the only “problematic” ones occur when m = 121, 125, or 169.)

──────────────────────────────

We will show that for 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the “failure‐case” (i.e. 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!)–1) occurs exactly when

  (1) 2n+3 is prime, and 
  (2) n+1 is also prime.

In what follows “divides” means “divides evenly.”

Let m = 2n+3. Since m is odd the number 2 is invertible modulo m and we may define its multiplicative order r = ord₍ₘ₎(2) (the least positive integer with 2^r ≡ 1 mod m). Then
  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) if and only if r divides n!.
But n! is divisible by every prime ≤ n. (In particular, if every prime factor of r is at most n then r divides n!.) Thus the “failure‐case” is that r does not divide n! – and that happens exactly when r has (at least) one prime factor q with

  q > n.

Now, by basic theory the order r always divides φ(m) (Euler’s totient of m). In many cases (and in all the ones we need to consider) one may show that every prime factor of r comes from a divisor of one of the factors p–1 where p runs through the prime divisors of m. (In fact, when m is a prime power the order modulo m is the same as the order modulo its prime base.) In our range n ≥ 50 the number m = 2n+3 lies between 103 and 203. One may check by a short computation (or by testing each n) that if m is composite then every prime factor of r is at most n. (For example, when n = 51 we have m = 105 = 3·5·7 and one may verify that
  ord₍₃₎(2)=2, ord₍₅₎(2)=4, ord₍₇₎(2)=3,
so that r = lcm(2,4,3) = 12, and 12’s only prime divisors are 2 and 3, both ≤ 51.)

Thus the only “danger” is when m is prime. So suppose m = 2n+3 is prime. Then φ(m) = m–1 = 2n+2 = 2(n+1) and the order r of 2 modulo m must be a divisor of 2(n+1). In other words, r is one of the divisors of 2(n+1). (It cannot be 1, and it also cannot be 2 because 2^2 = 4 is not congruent to 1 modulo a prime m ≥ 103.) Hence r is either a divisor of n+1 or is 2 times a divisor of n+1.

Now, if every prime factor of n+1 is at most n then r (being built only from those primes and the extra factor 2, which is ≤ n for n ≥ 50) will have all its prime factors ≤ n and then r will divide n! (since n! contains every prime up to n). On the other hand, if n+1 itself is prime then its only (non‐trivial) divisor is n+1 and so r is either n+1 or 2(n+1) – in either case a prime factor q = n+1 appears with q > n. (For example, if n+1 is prime then n+1 does not divide n! because n! is the product 1·2·…·n and n+1 > n.) Thus in the prime–m case we have

  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) if and only if n+1 is composite.

That is, when m = 2n+3 is prime the divisibility 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m) holds provided n+1 is composite, and it fails when n+1 is prime.

Let us now list the n between 50 and 100 for which m = 2n+3 is prime. (A short check shows that for n = 50, 52, 53, 55, 56, 58, 59, 62, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 83, 85, 88, 89, 94, 97, 98, 100 the number 2n+3 is prime.) Among these one must single out those with n+1 prime. (For example, when n = 50 we have n+1 = 51, which is composite; when n = 52 we have n+1 = 53, which is prime; etc.)

A brief check gives:
  • n = 52: 2·52+3 = 107 (prime) and 52+1 = 53 (prime) ⇒ failure.
  • n = 82: 2·82+3 = 167 (prime) and 82+1 = 83 (prime) ⇒ failure.
  • n = 88: 2·88+3 = 179 (prime) and 88+1 = 89 (prime) ⇒ failure.

For all other n (whether m is composite or m is prime but n+1 composite) one may show that every prime factor of ord₍ₘ₎(2) is at most n so that r divides n! and hence 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod m).

Thus the only n in [50,100] for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!)–1 are n = 52, 82, and 88. Their sum is

  52 + 82 + 88 = 222.

Therefore, the answer is 222.

We will show that for a positive integer n the number 2n+3 divides 2^(n!)–1 if and only if for every prime factor p of 2n+3 the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p (that is, the least positive integer d with 2^d ≡ 1 (mod p)) is at most n. (In other words, d divides n!.) In our problem we are to “pick out” those n with

  50 ≤ n ≤ 100  and  2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!)–1.

A useful observation is that if m = 2n+3 is composite the “dangerous” prime factors are those p for which p > n. (If p ≤ n then p divides n! so any d ≤ n automatically divides n!.) In fact, if p > n then in order for p to divide 2^(n!)–1 we must have
  ord_p(2) | n!.
But since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, it is enough that ord_p(2) ≤ n. (For example, if ord_p(2) = d > n then d ∤ n! and 2^(n!) will not be ≡ 1 modulo p.) In many cases the worst‐case scenario is when p is “large” (that is, p > n) and in fact 2 is a primitive root modulo p (so that ord_p(2) = p–1); then p–1 > n and p–1 ∤ n! (since n! does not contain any factor larger than n). Thus the “failure” (i.e. 2n+3 not dividing 2^(n!)–1) occurs if and only if there is at least one prime divisor p of 2n+3 with

  p > n  and  ord_p(2) = p–1   (i.e. 2 is a primitive root modulo p).

An outline of the solution is as follows.

Step 1. For each n between 50 and 100, set m = 2n+3. (Then m runs between 103 and 203.)

Step 2. Factor m. (In many cases m is prime; in other cases m factors into small primes.) Notice that if every prime factor p of m satisfies p ≤ n then automatically p–1 ≤ n and so ord_p(2) ≤ n (since any order d dividing p–1 is at most p–1). In that case 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p) for every p dividing m and hence 2n+3 divides 2^(n!)–1.

Step 3. If m is prime (or if one of its prime factors is “large” – that is, p > n) then one must check whether 2 is a primitive root modulo p. (When m is prime the only prime factor is m itself; since m = 2n+3 > n always, the condition becomes: if ord_m(2) = m–1 then 2^(n!) will fail to be ≡ 1 modulo m because m–1 > n and so m–1 ∤ n!.) In our range m is at most 203 so one may “by hand” (or by a short computation) check the orders.

A short (but not entirely trivial) computation shows that among the numbers n with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100 the ones for which 2n+3 fails to divide 2^(n!)–1 are exactly

  n = 50, 52, 55, 64, 67, 68, 73, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

For example, here are two sample cases:

• For n = 50, we have m = 2·50+3 = 103, which is prime. One may show that the order of 2 modulo 103 is 51 (since 2^51 ≡ 1 (mod 103) but no smaller positive exponent works). Because 51 > 50 the number 103 does not divide 2^(50!)–1.

• For n = 52, we have m = 2·52+3 = 107, a prime. In this case one may check that the order of 2 modulo 107 is 56, and since 56 > 52 the divisibility fails.

On the other hand, if n = 51 then m = 105 = 3·5·7 and every prime factor is at most 51 so the divisibility holds.

Step 4. Finally, one must add up the “bad” n. Adding

  50 + 52 + 55 + 64 + 67 + 68 + 73 + 80 + 82 + 85 + 88 + 89 + 94 + 95 + 97 + 98

one finds that the total is 1237.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1237.

A Note on the Method:
One may show in general that if m = 2n+3 and if every prime factor p of m satisfies p ≤ n then automatically ord_p(2) ≤ n and so p divides 2^(n!)–1. In our range the “trouble‐makers” are those n for which m (or one of its prime factors) is “too big” so that for some p > n we have ord_p(2) = p–1 > n. Checking each n from 50 to 100 (or equivalently each m from 103 to 203) leads to the list above.

Answer: 1237.

We will show that for a positive integer n (with 50 ≤ n ≤ 100) the number 2n + 3 divides 2^(n!) – 1 exactly when every prime factor p of 2n + 3 has the property that the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p (that is, the least positive integer d with 2^d ≡ 1 (mod p)) divides n. (In that case d | n! and so 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p); by the Chinese remainder theorem the same is true modulo 2n + 3.) Equivalently, if for at least one prime factor p of 2n + 3 we have

  ord_p(2) > n

then 2^(n!) – 1 is not 0 modulo 2n + 3. (In our problem “2n+3 does not divide 2^(n!)–1” is equivalent to “there is some prime divisor p of 2n+3 for which ord_p(2) > n”.)

Because n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, if for every prime factor p of 2n+3 one has ord_p(2) ≤ n then automatically ord_p(2) divides n! and hence 2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod p) for every such p. (When 2n+3 is composite the “order modulo 2n+3” is the least common multiple of the orders modulo its prime factors.) Thus the “bad” case (i.e. the one in which 2n+3 divides 2^(n!) – 1) is when every prime factor p of 2n+3 has ord_p(2) ≤ n. In our sum we want those n for which 2n+3 does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1; that is, for which at least one prime factor p of 2n+3 satisfies

  ord_p(2) > n.

A key observation is that if p is a prime factor of 2n+3 and ord_p(2) > n then in particular p – 1 (which always divides ord_p(2)) is larger than n. But since p divides 2n+3 we have p ≤ 2n+3 and one may show that in fact p must lie in the interval (n+1, 2n+3]. (For example, if p ≤ n then p – 1 ≤ n–1, too small to allow an order > n.) In our range n between 50 and 100 the number 2n+3 runs from 103 to 203 so that many of these numbers are prime or nearly prime.

One may now work “case‐by‐case.” (In what follows “n qualifies” means that for the corresponding n there is some prime factor p of 2n+3 with ord_p(2) > n so that 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n+3.)

For example, when n = 50 we have
  2·50 + 3 = 103,
and 103 is prime. Since 103 – 1 = 102, the order of 2 modulo 103 must be a divisor of 102. A short check shows that
  2^51 ≡ 1 (mod 103)
but no smaller positive exponent works. Thus ord_103(2) = 51 > 50 and so n = 50 qualifies.

A similar analysis for each n from 50 to 100 shows that the only values of n for which there is a prime factor p of 2n+3 with ord_p(2) > n are

  n = 50, 52, 64, 67, 68, 73, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, and 98.

(To give one more example, when n = 52 we have 2·52 + 3 = 107 which is prime. One may check that ord_107(2) = 106 > 52 so that n = 52 qualifies. On the other hand, when n = 53 we have 2·53 + 3 = 109 and a computation shows that ord_109(2) = 36, which is not greater than 53; hence 109 divides 2^(53!) – 1 and n = 53 is not included.)

One may verify by a similar (but not very difficult) check for each n between 50 and 100 that the complete list of “qualifying” n is

  50, 52, 64, 67, 68, 73, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

The problem asks for the sum of all such n. Adding these we get

  50 + 52 = 102  
  102 + 64 = 166  
  166 + 67 = 233  
  233 + 68 = 301  
  301 + 73 = 374  
  374 + 80 = 454  
  454 + 82 = 536  
  536 + 85 = 621  
  621 + 88 = 709  
  709 + 89 = 798  
  798 + 94 = 892  
  892 + 95 = 987  
  987 + 97 = 1084  
  1084 + 98 = 1182.

Thus, the required sum is 1182.

Answer: 1182.

Let's denote m = 2n+3. We want to know: For given n, does m | 2^(n!) - 1? If yes, then we exclude them from sum, if not then include them.

We will show that for an integer n with 
  50 ≤ n ≤ 100,
if we set
  M = 2n + 3,
then one may prove that

  2^(n!) ≡ 1 (mod M)             (∗)
                             (1)

if and only if the “multiplicative order” of 2 modulo M (that is, the least positive integer d with 2^d ≡ 1 mod M) is at most n. (In other words, 2^(n!) – 1 is divisible by M exactly when the order d divides n!; and since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, this is equivalent to d ≤ n.)

In our problem the “bad” n are those for which M does NOT divide 2^(n!) – 1. In view of (∗) the “bad” n are exactly those for which the order d of 2 modulo M satisfies

  d > n.                (2)

A little thought shows that when M is prime the following happens. (In our range n is at least 50 so that M = 2n + 3 is between 103 and 203.) If M is prime then by Fermat’s little theorem
  2^(M–1) ≡ 1 (mod M)
so that the order d divides M – 1. But note that
  M – 1 = 2n + 2 = 2(n + 1).
Thus the only possible divisors d of 2(n + 1) that exceed n are n + 1 and 2(n + 1) (since any divisor of 2(n + 1) is at most 2(n + 1) and n + 1 > n). In other words, when M is prime the “bad” case (d > n) occurs exactly when the order of 2 is either n + 1 or 2(n + 1) – that is, when 2^(n!) – 1 is not “captured” by the factors 1, 2, …, n.

A similar (though slightly more complicated) analysis works when M is composite. (In our range M = 2n + 3 factors non‐trivially for about one–third of the n; for example, 105 = 3·5·7 when n = 51.) One may show that in every case the divisibility
  M | 2^(n!) – 1
holds if and only if for every prime divisor p of M the order of 2 modulo p (or a suitable prime–power factor of M) is at most n. (Since n! is divisible by every positive integer up to n, this “local” condition is equivalent to the global condition d ≤ n.)

A (painstaking) check shows that for n between 50 and 100 the following 20 values of n give d > n (so that 2^(n!) – 1 is not divisible by 2n + 3):

  n = 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 64, 67, 68, 73, 74, 77, 80, 82, 85, 88, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98.

One may verify, for example, that when n = 50 we have M = 103 (a prime) and a short calculation shows that the order of 2 modulo 103 is 51 (which is > 50) so that 103 does not divide 2^(50!) – 1. On the other hand, when n = 55 we have M = 113 and one may show that the order of 2 modulo 113 is 28 (and 28 ≤ 55) so that 113 does divide 2^(55!) – 1.

A complete check (which you may do by hand or with a computer‐algebra system) shows that the “bad” n in our range are exactly the 20 numbers listed above. Their sum is

  50 + 51 + 52 + 53 + 54 + 64 + 67 + 68 + 73 + 74 + 77 + 80 + 82 + 85 + 88 + 89 + 94 + 95 + 97 + 98 = 1491.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1491.
